CITY  OF  ALHAMBRA

  REGULARMEETING OF THE
  ALHAMBRA HOUSING AND COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT
  CITIZEN ADVISORY COMMITTEE

The Regular Meeting of the Alhambra Housing and Community Development Citizen
Advisory (HCDA) Committee will be held on Tuesday, October 6, 2020, commencing
at 7:00 p.m. via teleconference and video conference.

  CORONAVIRUS (COVID-19) ADVISORY NOTICE

Consistent with Executive Orders No. N-29-20 and No. N-35-20 from the Executive
Department of the State of California and the County of Los Angeles Department of Public
Health Safer At Home Order, the Alhambra Housing and Community Development
Citizen Advisory Committee meeting will not be physically open to the public and the
meeting will take place via teleconference and video conference.

To watch and listen to the meeting: To maximize public safety while still maintaining
transparency and public access, members of the public can participate by using Zoom
Meeting as follows:

Zoom direct link:

https://us02web.zoom.us/j/87674862417?pwd=YXdRLy93RnA4dzhZKzJzQ1huMDFP
QT09

Webinar ID: 876 7486 2417

Passcode: 843111

Or by telephone by dialing: 1-888-475-4499 (Toll Free) or 1-833-548-0276 (Toll Free) or
1-833-548-0282 (Toll Free) or 1-877-853-5257 (Toll Free)

Webinar ID: 876 7486 2417 and Passcode: 843111

Please Note: All members of the public calling or logging into the meeting will be muted
so that the meeting can proceed. For those wishing to speak on an agenda item, please
email Matthew Cuevas at mcuevas@cityofalhambra.org by 5:00 p.m. prior to the meeting
with the item number you wish to speak on and the phone number you will use when
calling or the name you will use when logging into the meeting. You should then call or
log into the meeting at least 5 minutes prior to its start time. Staff will unmute you and
announce you when it is your time to speak. You will have five minutes to speak, unless
that time is adjusted by the meeting Chair. Given the challenges of teleconference and
video conference meetings, all participants are encouraged to email their comments
prior to the beginning of the meeting.
 Comments can be emailed to the Matthew Cuevas at mcuevas@cityofalhambra.org by no
later than 5:00 p.m. on October 6, 2020 to ensure there is sufficient time to print the emails
prior to the beginning of the meeting. Comments will then be read into the record, with a
maximum allowance of 5 minutes per individual comment, subject to the Chair’s
discretion. If a comment is received after 5:00 p.m. but before the conclusion of the
meeting based upon its time stamp, the comment will still be included as a part of the
record of the meeting but will not be read into the record.

An agenda of the regular meeting is attached hereto incorporated herein by reference and
made a part hereof as though fully set forth herein.
   AGENDA
  REGULAR MEETING
HOUSING AND COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT CITIZEN ADVISORY COMMITTEE
  TUESDAY, OCTOBER 6, 2020 AT 7:00 P.M.

1. ROLL CALL:
  Bill Vallejos, Chair  Mark Lee, Vice Chair
  Bonita Sharma-Ngan  Andrea Giese
  Marc Tousignant  Sasha Renée Pérez
  Maria Conchita Bañuelos  Yvette Cardenas
  Marcos Sayon

2. MINUTES
  Approval of the minutes for the Regular Meeting of August 4, 2020.
  Approval of the minutes for the Regular Meeting of September 1, 2020.

3. PROGRESS REPORTS
  Attached for the Committee’s review are copies of the Progress Reports for those programs
  utilizing Community Development Block Grant and HOME Funds. All figures indicate the
  progress made and services rendered to date for FY 2020-2021.
   Parks and Recreation - Case Management
   66 Case Management clients were served.
   0 Volunteer Hours of assistance were donated to the program.
   Community Development - Code Enforcement
   The Code Enforcement Division investigated a total of 115 complaints.
   15 were identified as confirmed complaints as stand-alone Health & Safety Issues.
   Code Enforcement staff referred 28 to the Housing Department programs.
   Community Development - Fair Housing
   The Housing Rights Center served approx. 35 clients.
   A variety of issues were discussed, including: evictions, security deposits, rent
  increases, repairs, contract questions, etc.
   Community Development - Housing Programs
   First-Time Home Buyer - HOME: 10 searching for a home, 0 escrow closed.
   HOME Major Rehabilitation: 2 in process, 0 completed.
   CDBG Minor Rehabilitation: 2 in process, 0 completed.

  Recommended Action
  Receive and file these informational reports.

4. PRESENTATION FROM CITY’S HOMELESS OUTREACH PROVIDER – LOS
  ANGELES CENTERS FOR ALCOHOL AND DRUG ABUSE (L.A. CADA)
  A representative with the Los Angeles Centers for Alcohol and Drug Abuse (L.A. CADA)
  will provide a brief presentation regarding the Alhambra Homeless Outreach and Mental
  Evaluation (H.O.M.E.) efforts, including contacting, assessing, and working with individuals
  with substance abuse to accept housing and treatment. L.A. CADA will also discuss their
  support services to the homeless community, including their approach to persons and
  families within Alhambra experiencing homelessness.
   Recommended Action
  Receive and file presentation.

5. COMMENTS FROM THE AUDIENCE
  Discussion from the public of any item not specified on the agenda. Comments must pertain
  to the business of the HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee. Public comments pertaining to
  the HCDA Committee’s business are welcome. Kindly limit all oral communications to five
  (5) minutes. Please complete the blue speaker card prior to the meeting and submit it to the
  Committee’s secretary.

6. COMMENTS AND CONCERNS FROM THE COMMITTEE
  Discussion from the Committee Members of any item(s) not specified on the agenda. Items
  discussed must pertain to the business of the HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee.

7. ADJOURNMENT

 Copies of the staff report or other written documentation relating to each item of business described herein
 above are on file in the office of Management Services, Alhambra City Hall, 111 S. First Street, Alhambra,
 CA, and are available for public inspection during regular office hours: 7:00 A.M. to 12:00 P.M., Monday
 through Thursday.
 Should any person have a question concerning any of the above agenda items prior to the meeting described
 herein, he or she may contact Mr. Matthew Cuevas, Management Analyst, either in person, at the
 Management Services Department located at City Hall, or call via telephone at (626) 570-5011, during
 regular business hours.

 Americans with Disabilities Act: If you require special assistance to participate in any City meeting, please
 contact the City Clerk's Office (626) 570-5090. Notification of at least 72 hours prior to the meeting will
 enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to ensure accessibility to this meeting.
   UNOFFICIAL
  Minutes of the City of Alhambra’s
  HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee
  Regular Meeting of August 4, 2020
  MEETING CONDUCTED VIA TELECONFERENCE/ZOOM DUE TO COVID-19.

  Assistant City Manager Garcia called the meeting to order at 7:05 p.m.

1. ROLL CALL:
  Committee Members Present:
  Maria Conchita Bañuelos  Andrea Giese
  Marc Tousignant  Bonita Sharma-Ngan
  Sasha Renée Pérez  Marcos Sayon
  Yvette Cardenas

  Committee Members Absent:
  Bill Vallejos
  Mark Lee

  City Staff Present:
  Lucy Garcia, Assistant City Manager
  Matthew Cuevas, Management Analyst
  Rafael Perez, Code Enforcement Supervisor
  Chancela Al-Mansour, Executive Director, Housing Rights Center

2. MINUTES
  The Committee reviewed the minutes for the Special Meeting of June 16, 2020. Committee
  Member Cardenas requested a minor change on page 2 of the June 16, 2020 minutes.
  Assistance City Manager Garcia stated that change will be made on the official minutes.

  Committee Action:
  Committee Member Bañuelos moved, seconded by Committee Member Tousignant, to
  approve the minutes for the Special Meeting of June 16, 2020 with the requested change.
  Ayes:  Bañuelos, Giese, Sharma-Ngan, Sayon, Tousignant, Pérez and Cardenas.
  Noes:  None.
  Abstain: None.

3. PROGRESS REPORTS
  The Committee reviewed the reports. All figures indicate the progress made and services
  rendered to date for FY 2019-2020. Assistant City Manager Garcia gave an overview of the
  current progress reports for each program area.

  Committee Member Pérez asked for clarification on how HUD funds are used for Code
  Enforcement regarding extreme issues renters are faced with. She spoke about a recent
  incident where a family contacted her and had no electricity or gas since the 4th of July. She
  stated the family had reached out to both Code Enforcement and the Housing Rights Center
  but was unable to get any assistance. The family’s situation was resolved when the Los
  Angeles County Health Department was contacted and a health violation was issued.
  Committee Member Pérez inquired what types of situations does Code Enforcement step in.

  Page 1 of 10
   Assistant City Manager Garcia responded that was a good question and was a good lead into
  the presentations. Assistant City Manager Garcia then introduced Executive Director Al-
  Mansour of the Housing Rights Center.

  Committee Action:
  The Committee received and filed these informational reports.

4. PRESENTATIONS FROM HOUSING RIGHTS CENTER AND CODE
  ENFORCEMENT
  Executive Director Al-Mansour introduced herself and responded to Committee Member
  Pérez that she was not aware of this particular case. She went over the Housing Rights
  Center’s intake and case management process, and how certain cases are referred to Code
  Enforcement. She reiterated the Housing Rights Center’s commitment to serving clients and
  would look further into this particular instance.

  Executive Director Al-Mansour began her presentation regarding the Housing Rights Center.
  The presentation provided brief background on the Housing Rights Center and the multitude
  of services that are provided and included an overview of the Fair Housing Act. She then
  discussed the effects COVID-19 has had on eviction moratoriums under the California
  Judicial Council’s emergency rule, and local laws and how each city has its own type of
  moratorium order.

  Executive Director Al-Mansour then talked about how COVID-19 changed the way the
  Housing Rights Center is able to provide its services, but noted it has allowed for more
  specialized trainings on eviction moratoriums, housing discrimination, and seminars on
  mental health and ADA reasonable accommodations during COVID-19. Executive Director
  Al-Mansour added the Housing Rights Center also assists landlords with housing issues. She
  concluded her presentation by sharing the Housing Rights Center’s weekly activities
  schedule and stated they were going to do more virtual services to assist clients.

  Committee Member Pérez asked if the weekly schedule in the presentation was on the
  Housing Rights Center’s website and if the only hours currently offered were during mid-
  day.

  Executive Director Al-Mansour answered the weekly schedule and other resources are
  available on the website. She also stated they are currently reaching out to cities individually
  about hours, the types of clinics being offered and suggestions for each community on what
  their needs are. Executive Director Al-Mansour added the Housing Rights Center did offer
  clinics on Saturdays earlier in the year but stopped hosting those due to low attendance. She
  said the Housing Rights Center is looking at extending evening hours.

  Assistant City Manager Garcia inquired about possible backlogs of cases.

  Executive Director Al-Mansour answered the Housing Rights Center strives to return all calls
  within a 48-hour period. She stated intake staff who answer phone calls try to get as much
  information as possible including email addresses, how many times a client has called and on
  which days. Executive Director Al-Mansour also indicated that sometimes clients who do not
  receive an immediate response will often say they did not receive any call back.

  Committee Member Pérez stated she had been contacted by approximately a dozen
  individuals who said they called the 800 number for the Housing Rights Center but never
  Page 2 of 10
 received a call back. She stated one individual told her they did not receive a response until a
week later. Committee Member Pérez mentioned the current clinic time slots may not be
convenient for working people to attend since they are in the middle of the day. She
suggested exploring the possibility of hosting in-person clinics, while maintaining social
distancing guidelines, and felt it was valuable to have someone come to the City at least once
a month to provide assistance in-person.

Executive Director Al-Mansour responded she would look into the intake sheets, and they try
to call clients back repeatedly but there may be instances when the clients do not receive the
call back messages. She stated there was a recent change to the intake phone system to focus
on both the most recent calls and also the calls from repeat phone numbers. Executive
Director Al-Mansour reiterated when intake staff receives messages, they take down names,
phone numbers and have a staff member call the person back immediately. She stated she
wants to know when there are communication issues so the Housing Rights Center can solve
the problem quickly. Executive Director Al-Mansour also said they are looking into offering
different times for workshop hours.

Committee Member Pérez noted that City Hall had recently opened for limited hours and
suggested having someone on site for an hour in the morning, or possibly using empty office
space to meet with residents. Another suggestion put forward Committee Member Pérez was
to have a tent set up outside if that would be safer and it would also help residents.

Executive Director Al-Mansour indicated she would entertain that suggestion but felt that it
would be more useful if it wasn’t just Housing Rights Center staff but also Code
Enforcement officers available as well to assist residents with housing issues.

Committee Member Pérez agreed but said she was concerned about the lack of coordination
between the Housing Rights Center and Code Enforcement regarding this instance where a
family had no electricity during this heat and had to use dry ice since their refrigerator did
not work. She stated thankfully Los Angeles County stepped in to help, but for the family not
to get assistance from the Housing Rights Center and Code Enforcement was concerning.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez agreed to attending workshops and interfacing with
clients and citizens to solve issues. He reiterated Code Enforcement’s commitment to the
partnership with Housing Rights Center in solving issues.

Assistant City Manager Garcia stated having workshops at City Hall would be discussed later
to make the appointments happen.

Committee Member Pérez asked if she could get Executive Director Al-Mansour’s email
address.

Executive Director Al-Mansour replied she would provide that.

Assistant City Manager Garcia introduced Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez began his presentation on the role of the Code
Enforcement Division regarding CDBG funding. Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez
provided a general overview of the areas Code Enforcement is responsible for including
things such as landscaping, graffiti, and substandard living conditions. He also spoke about
  Page 3 of 10
 the internal stakeholders the division coordinates regarding other City departments and the
external stakeholders and partnerships with other agencies.

In responding to Committee Member Pérez’s inquiry about the family with no electricity, he
noted the City does not have a rental inspection program and without this tool, the City relies
heavily on the Los Angeles County Health Department to handles those types of inspections.
Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez also spoke about the other county departments the City
coordinates with. He reiterated the partnership with the Housing Rights Center and providing
information to tenants regarding landlord/tenant issues or any other housing rights violations.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez then explained that only serious health and safety issues
qualify as violations under CDBG funding. He explained these violations were things such as
peeling paint on the exterior, major structural issues and other hazardous conditions. Code
Enforcement Supervisor Perez provided examples to the Committee, as well as the various
Code violations that do not qualify under CDBG such as landscaping and litter. He stated that
landscaping and litter violations would be ancillary to the health and safety violations. Code
Enforcement Supervisor Perez also reviewed the number of complaints the Code
Enforcement Division received to date, and noted that only 84 were stand alone health and
safety violations that qualified under CDBG.

Committee Member Pérez inquired if the numbers are just reported to the City of Alhambra.
She referred back to the example of the family that contacted the County and asked if that
gets communicated back to the City and if the City tracks that.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez responded in this instance it resulted from a fire that
occurred on July 4 and his office was not contacted until July 21. He stated once the division
was notified, Code Enforcement responded and took photos of the unit. Code Enforcement
Supervisor Perez said a notice was not issued at the time since Code Enforcement wanted to
get further assistance from the City’s Fire Prevention and Building Divisions. He stated all
the divisions returned the next day and issued notices of violations. Code Enforcement
Supervisor Perez also mentioned he has stayed in communication with the family since July
21 to follow up. He stated since there is no rental inspection program or City laws in place,
the City cannot provide mandated emergency housing and impose that on a property owner,
and as a result the family was referred to Los Angeles County for further assistance. Code
Enforcement Supervisor Perez further explained that in this instance the referral to the Los
Angeles County Health Department is what triggered the mechanism for the emergency
housing while the owner mitigated the issues. He restated since the City does not have a
rental housing inspection program, Code Enforcement does not have the tools to impose on a
landlord a requirement to house families who have been displaced, in instances such as this,
at a separate location; however, the owner was instructed to work with the tenants to obtain
the necessary assistance.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez continued his presentation and provided examples of
violations that qualify under the CDBG program. He noted that stand alone issues such as
landscaping, trash and vehicles parked on front lawns do not qualify as violations under
CDBG, but are considered routine code violations that would fall under the General Fund
source. Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez described the various enforcement methods up
to administrative citations and criminal prosecution, which he noted were rarely used but is
an available tool Code Enforcement has. He reiterated that Code Enforcement always looks
for education and compliance before issuing citations. He then discussed hoarding situations
and stated the division works with outside groups to assist, as well as coordinating with the
  Page 4 of 10
 homeowner or landlord to address the issue, and make referrals to the Los Angeles County
Department of Mental Health if the situation calls for it.

Committee Member Pérez inquired about one of the examples in the presentation of a private
garage and how Code Enforcement would address that since it is private property and the
garage door closes.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez responded if the garage door is open, and Code
Enforcement has received compliant, they would investigate. He noted in this instance an
illegal automotive repair shop was being run out of this residential garage. Code Enforcement
Supervisor Perez said there are 33 sections under the City Code that violations can be
addressed, and Code Enforcement will continue to address any issues to mitigate complaints
but stated the only time Code Enforcement would not get involved is a civil matter.

Committee Member Pérez mentioned at last night’s Planning Commission meeting the issue
of certain permitted conditions for developments being set, but then the conditions are
ignored, and asked if Code Enforcement played a role to ensure that any set conditions are
honored.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez responded that the development conditions are done
through the Planning Department and entitlement process, and no active enforcement for
entitlements is conducted unless a complaint is received. He stated City planners assign
requirements to check-in and perform inspections, and if they find an issue they will mitigate
it or refer it Code Enforcement for action. Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez explained that
Code Enforcement is not involved in the step by step process for a project regarding
entitlements.

Committee Member Pérez asked what happens if it is discovered that a project is out of
compliance with entitlements.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez replied that Code Enforcement can issue an immediate
stop work order and some of the additional tools for enforcement action can lead up to civil
prosecution or fines. He said Code Enforcement will use tools at their disposal for the
enforcement of policy.

Committee Member Pérez stated that Director Castagnola has said it was difficult to check if
developer was out of compliance and is able to get away with it.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez replied if a developer is not complying, would need to
look at that during the development process and speak with his Director regarding Code
Enforcement’s role, and see if Code Enforcement can have a better supplement to those
issues. He then continued his presentation discussing the role Code Enforcement plays in
regards to community policing and crime prevention, and coordinating with the Police
Department and the HOME Team to address illegal encampments and provide help to
homeless individuals.

Committee Member Pérez asked about one of the images in the presentation if the location
was next to the old Wahib’s restaurant?

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez explained what happened to the property regarding a
previous fire and subsequent insurance issues.
  Page 5 of 10
 Committee Member Pérez stated it was an old, historic brick building and asked if there was
no other option to save it aside from demolishing it.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez explained in detail how the abandoned building became
a public nuisance and led to trespassing and graffiti issues, and it was diverting police
department patrol resources due to officers constantly having to patrol the burned-out
building. He also stated even after boarding up and placing a fence around the property, it did
not deter trespassers and they had to weigh the health and safety aspect with waiting for the
planning entitlements to be approved, so the property owner could take his time to rebuild. In
light of this, the decision was made to move forward with the demolition of the burned-out
building.

Committee Member Pérez asked if the department had sole oversight to force the demolition
without any other approval such as the City Council. She referenced the city of Los Angeles
that has the ability to restore old historic buildings that also suffered from fire damage but
were able to be repaired.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez said he was giving an overview of the situation, but
there were many other things going on behind the scenes coordinating with other
departments. He stated if the building was identified by the Planning Division as historic, it
would not have mandated the building be demolished. Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez
indicated in this situation that wasn’t the case, the City would like to protect certain
buildings, but if the evidence supported the health and safety issues, on a case by case basis,
but will continue to work with other departments. He finished his presentation by providing
an overview of Annual Neighborhood Clean Up event coordinated by Code Enforcement.

Committee Member Pérez stated she wanted to make sure she understood what Code
Enforcement takes care of versus what the Housing Rights Center takes care of. She
mentioned the issue with the Perez family she brought up earlier, and asked if the County had
not filed their own separate warning, if the landlord has not acted, then Code Enforcement
would have taken further actions.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez responded yes, Code Enforcement would have taken
additional action to get the owner to make the improvements and mitigate the issues. He
stated if the owner would have deviated form that, Code Enforcement has the ability to
undertake additional enforcement action.

Committee Member Pérez inquired if Code Enforcement would continue to check up on
compliance efforts or if it is up to the resident.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez answered that Code Enforcement would follow up on
each violation. He stated that the division gives short time frames to comply with major
health and safety violations and longer time frames for more minor violations, but will
always follow up on each violation.

Committee Member Pérez stated she was happy things are getting resolved. She asked for
clarification purposes, in a situation where there is a dispute with rent, if that’s when the
Housing Rights Center would step-in. Committee Member Pérez asked if a list can be created
that shows what Code Enforcement takes care of and what the Housing Rights Center takes
care of as a flyer for those who need it, and also maybe post the flyer online to help them
  Page 6 of 10
 better navigate.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez replied that Code Enforcement is working with the
Housing Rights Center and the legal department on what is a code case versus an issue a
tenant has to address civilly with the landlord before it is turned over to code for
enforcement. He reiterated any time Code Enforcement gets a complaint they will look at it
and see if it’s something they need to respond to, or if they need to make a referral and
initiate that process. Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez stated they always offer those
resources to citizens who are experiencing those issues.

Committee Member Pérez said it was helpful to have some of these things more defined. She
spoke again about the situation with the Perez family and repeated they had contacted Code
Enforcement on July 6 but maybe they did not accurately explain the situation that would
have triggered a code enforcement violation. Committee Member Pérez noted these resources
would be very helpful to renters and them knowing their rights especially now during these
times so they aren’t worried about losing their housing.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez replied that Code Enforcement is absolutely committed
to doing that and working with the Housing Rights Center in providing those resources.

Committee Member Cardenas commented in light of a current situation in the city of Los
Angeles, easing up on code enforcement for some businesses that received fines for having
signs advertising their business or services until Mayor Garcetti stepped in and interceded.
She expressed concerned a similar thing can happen with home owners and landlords and the
last thing the City should be doing is having people repaint their house because of paint
chipping. Committee Member Cardenas implied these are the times to let those things slide
because people are in financial peril.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez responded that when the COVID shutdown happened,
he spoke with his Director and a decision was made to not fine businesses regarding banners
and signage as long as it met established guidelines, and was not a health and safety issue. He
stated while he understands a large portion of businesses have been impacted, any handicap
accessibility issues would override the signage and banner requirement relaxation. Code
Enforcement Supervisor Perez said he wanted to be flexible with businesses and to allow
outdoor dining in order to help out businesses in the City. He stated in regards to dealing with
vacant businesses and housing in general, they would work with homeowners but there isn’t
a database that tells Code Enforcement if the owner is experiencing some type of struggles.
Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez noted they are finding people are home more due to
quarantine and they are receiving more complaints from residents, but are remining flexible
for minor violations during COVID-19 unless it’s a major health and safety issue. He
provided the example of overgrown vegetation and noted that Code Enforcement’s first
reaction is not to issue fines and citations, but will issue an informational flyer and help work
to find a solution, and in this particular instance they ended up going back out and cutting the
vegetation. Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez again reiterated they are not looking to
impose fines and will be flexible, unless its an issue that’s health and safety.

Committee Member Cardenas asked for more clarification that decisions are being made on
call by call basis, if there is no policy during this time period.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez answered that was correct. He reiterated they are
working with their Director, who oversees Code Enforcement, and it’s his decision when
  Page 7 of 10
   they can flexible and when they need to take enforcement action.

  Committee Action:
  The Committee received and filed these informational presentations.

5. COMMENTS FROM THE AUDIENCE
  None.

6. COMMENTS AND CONCERNS FROM THE COMMITTEE
  Assistant City Manager Garcia informed the Committee that in preparation for the CAPER, it
  will be submitted to the Committee prior to the City Council and will be on the agenda for
  the next meeting.

  Committee Member Pérez asked Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez for his email address.

  Code Enforcement Supervisor Perez provided both his email address and the generic Code
  Enforcement email address.

  Committee Member Bañuelos thanked Officer Perez and the Housing Rights Center for the
  times she has called or referred people to them. She thanked staff for trying to accommodate
  the Committee during these times but would like to be more active and provide a list of
  resources to residents who need assistance.

  Committee Member Cardenas inquired about the January 7 meeting minutes missing from
  the website and if staff can look into that. She also expressed concern about the Consolidated
  Plan’s analysis on housing and economic conditions, and for the bulk of the meetings only
  one public comment was received, and indicated all the meetings occurred pre-COVID and
  the information dealt with those conditions, and noted it wouldn’t be fair to use this
  information from 2019 for the next five years prior to when so much had occurred.
  Committee Member Cardenas stated it didn’t seem like recovery will be quick, she
  mentioned Councilmember Lee had brough up concerns about tenants after the eviction
  moratoriums expire and how to help re-house tenants, and would like more information on
  rapid rehousing assistance.

  Committee Member Cardenas stated an issue is the rent hike freezes and eviction
  moratoriums will end and we’ll see landlords increase rents. She also spoke about issues with
  EDD and mentioned she applied in April but has not received any assistance in five months,
  and has been utilizing her savings to pay her bills. Committee Member Cardenas also
  mentioned the difficulty of having no childcare since March and the current available options
  are limited for her child, coupled with following health guidance on not mixing households
  makes grandparents not an option.

  Committee Member Cardenas expressed concern about the inclusionary housing ordinance
  and needing to make sure its affordable for low income residents to purchase a place. She
  stated in January it was decided to take away the first-time home buyer program, and noted at
  the last meeting Ms. Tam had indicated it was removed because housing is very expensive to
  purchase in the city, but Committee Member Cardenas felt with the inclusionary housing
  ordinance it would make housing more affordable. Committee Member Cardenas said she
  felt the Consolidated Plan for the next five years is out of date and the Committee needs to
  revisit the information and do another analysis.

  Page 8 of 10
 Assistant City Manager Garcia stated that although the Consolidated Plan is for five years,
there are yearly action plans when it can be amended. She stated there are options to amend
and that can be agendized for a future meeting for discussion. Assistant City Manager Garcia
also stated that rapid rehousing and what that entails, and if it would be available, can also be
agendized to discuss at a future meeting.

Committee Member Cardenas inquired if City Council had the ability to make changes to the
document if it has not been approved yet.

Assistant City Manager Garcia responded the document was currently out for review and
public comment.

Committee Member Cardenas asked how would the public would know it’s available for
review.

Assistant City Manager Garcia explained a public notice was published in several
newspapers and online. She also noted it would be included with the staff report as an
attachment.

Committee Member Cardenas asked to verify the newspapers it was published in and also
where online it was posted.

Management Analyst Cuevas responded the notice was published in the Pasadena Star News,
La Opinión and World Journal newspapers. He also stated the plan was posted on the City’s
website for review.

Committee Member Cardenas inquired about agendizing those future items for discussion.

Assistant City Manager Garcia asked all Committee Members if there was any interest in
pursing the request to agendize future items for discussion. She noted there needed to be a
second from another Committee Member.

Committee Member Pérez also inquired about how to agendize items for future meetings.

Assistant City Manager Garcia suggested waiting a few meetings until the current pandemic
plays out and revisit the plan in approximately six to seven months.

Committee Member Pérez stated she would be ok with revisiting at the next meeting if it
allowed for time to review and discuss it.

Committee Member Cardenas indicated she had questions and wanted to learn more about
rapid rehousing assistance and the Consolidated Plan process. She asked if the plan could be

4. 2019-2020 CONSOLIDATED ANNUAL PERFORMANCE AND EVALUATION
  REPORT (CAPER)
  Assistant City Manager Garcia gave an overview of what encompasses the Consolidated
  Page 1 of 6
 Annual Performance Evaluation Report (CAPER). She discussed the Goals and Outcomes
section of the CAPER in relation to all the City’s activities and the national objectives and
goals. Assistant City Manager Garcia also stated this CAPER reported on the last year of the
2015 – 2019 Consolidated Plan, and next year’s CAPER will cover year one of the City’s
recently adopted Consolidated Plan. Assistant City Manager Garcia reviewed the primary
accomplishments contained in the report:

  •  HOME Housing Minor Rehabilitation - 1 project underway.
  •  CDBG funded Minor Rehabilitation - 1 project underway.
  •  First Time Home Buyer - 2 households’ closed escrow, 9 households sought a home,
  and 7 households sought assistance.
  •  CHDO - in conjunction with support from the Housing Asset Fund, the City
  rehabilitated and expanded a 3-bedfroom property unit in 2019 utilizing both CHDO
  and First Time Home Buyer program.
  •  Code Enforcement – 929 violations were investigated and 576 were located in the
  low-moderate areas as required by CDBG program guidelines. Additionally, 553
  referrals were made to the housing rehabilitation program/Housing Rights Center.
  Assistant City Manager Garcia reminded the Committee that Code Enforcement had
  changed the way statistics were compiled for the new Consolidated Plan and 500
  violations in the target area is the now the target goal and will monitored moving
  forward.

Assistant City Manager Garcia then discussed the equal housing opportunity program under
fair housing services and any HUD funded capital improvement efforts during the program
year and noted:

  •  Fair Housing Services – 318 clients were served in Alhambra. Of those clients, 4
  percent required assistance with housing discrimination and the remainder required
  general housing services.

  •  Capital Improvement Program – prior year project regarding street rehabilitation
  program that was spent in 2019 and benefited 950 individuals who lived in that
  project’s particular low-moderate area census tract. In addition, 6 other public
  improvements were also combined to provide a public benefit to other low-moderate
  income areas.

Assistant City Manager Garcia then reviewed the Case Management Program, Housing, and
Administration efforts that included:

  •  Case Management – 105 new clients, 439 reassurance calls made, and 4,000 meals
  were served in the 2019 year
  •  Commercial Rehabilitation – no major economic development activities, as it was
  deemed a low priority need during the development of the Consolidated Plan.
  •  Planning and Administration – staff time to monitor and implement CDBG and
  HOME programs.

Assistant City Manager Garcia then briefly discussed a section of the report that outlines the
different activities funded by CDBG and HOME and the categories and goals they fulfill.
She noted the majority of the City’s goals were met with the exception of homeowner
housing rehabilitation program, which came in at 33 percent served. Assistant City Manager
  Page 2 of 6
 Garcia stated that although the number appeared low, she stated the City given the nuances of
this year, it is expected the activity will improve by the end of 2021. She stated the report
currently does not contain the amount expended during the program year since the City is
still going through the accruals between the 19-20 fiscal year, but they will be completed in
time to present to City Council and send to HUD.

Assistant City Manager Garcia touched on other needs outlined in the CAPER relating to
homelessness and the City has contracted with a new provider, LACADA, to assume
navigation, case management work and crisis sheltering referrals and will apply to the new
fiscal year and Consolidated plan. She noted these new services are not being funded through
CDBG funds but through the Housing Successor Asset fund and other grant funding sources.

Veronica Tam, Veronica Tam and Associates, clarified public improvement projects are
really 6 major locations throughout the City under one larger, umbrella project. She also
stated in this year’s CAPER, activities under the CDBG COVID funds, such as COVID-19
testing, senior meals and emergency housing assistance would be included (statuses). Ms.
Tam further stated the findings to the Analysis of Impediments to Fair Housing Choice
would also be incorporated into this year’s CAPER since it was prepared during the 2019
fiscal year.

typically submitted in September; however, HUD has extended the submission deadline to
January 2021; nonetheless, the City has elected to proceed with a September submittal.
